newsitem.title: INDIA: BSE sees India markets buoyant on new tax rules.
newsitem.headline: BSE sees India markets buoyant on new tax rules.

text.p: Attractive new tax provisions in India's 1997/98 budget will fuel primary market activity and cause interest rates to drop, Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) president Madan Gopal Damani said on Monday.
"There has been a sea change in the minds of the people," Damani told a news conference. "This is clearly shown in the number of trades pouring in after the post-budget session."

India's broking community responded enthusaistically to the provisions of the budget, with the 30-share BSE index climbing to 4007.91 on Monday, before falling back to close provisionally at 3,870.34.
Damani said he expected the index to climb to 5,000 points by October, in time for Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights.

"If the moonson is good, by Diwali, I expect the index to reach 5,000. This is being conservative," Damani said. "It will be a slow, steady rise. The biggest beneficiary would be the individual investor."
In the next two or three months, he said, he saw it putting on about half that rise.
"I think it will get halfway there during the next three or four months, that is about 4,500," Damani added.
"It was suggested after the budget that the bull charge would be led by the FIIs (Foreign Institutional Investors), but I begged to differ," Damani said.
"I said investors would be coming in large numbers, and within 24 hours this was reflected in the number of trades."
The government's decision not to tax dividends as investor income had boosted individual investor sentiment, Damani said.

Another damper for industry, the Minimum Alternate Tax, introduced last year to net firms that paid no tax on profits because they put funds into new projects, had been converted into a minimum advance tax.

"I think not more than two or three percent of companies will be hit by MAT after the amendment," Damani said. "And I think market sentiment will not change if only two or three percent are affected."

The budget's moves on personal income tax -- it lopped ten percentage points off every category -- coupled with a scheme to legalise undeclared income at a fixed rate of 30 percent will draw the small investor into the stock markets, Damani said.
"I expect the primary market to revive within three months from now, considering what has happened to the secondary market," he added.
"Responses to new issues will be much much better than one can think of. This will be the biggest change in the outlook of the capital market."

The budget also permitted two of India's largest financial institutions, the Life Insurance Corp of India and the Unit Trust of India, to launch pension schemes. Damani expected these funds to help boost the stockmarkets.
Many non-resident Indians (NRIs) had expressed interest in investing in India in the weekend following the budget presentation, he added.
"In the last three days, I've received 40 or 50 calls from NRIs, asking me to come and explain to them the opportunities available for investment," Damani said.

"They will find it convenient to come to India," an ebullient Damani said. "The liquidity problem will be a matter of history. All you have to do is convert the dollars into rupees and it will be ready for deployment."
Under the impact of the inflow of funds -- which he estimated to be in the range of several billion dollars -- interest rates would come down, Damani said.
"I expect interest rates to come down three percent this year," Damani said. "Three percent is a hell of a lot of money, because interest runs 24 hours a day."
